title: Thermal Properties of Matter
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Thermometry, Thermal Expansion (Linear, Area, Volume, Pendulums & Thermal Stress), Calorimetry, Phase Changes, Heat Conduction, Radiation (Stefan-Boltzmann & Wien's Laws) & Newton's Law of Cooling
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: What Is the Difference Between Temperature and Heat?

In everyday conversation, people use the words heat and temperature interchangeably. In Physics, they are two completely different concepts!

Temperature vs. Heat:
• Temperature ($T$): A measure of the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules inside a body. It decides the direction of spontaneous thermal energy flow (always from higher $T$ to lower $T$).
• Heat ($Q$): Thermal energy in transit that flows from one body to another solely due to a temperature difference between them. A body never “contains” heat—it contains Internal Energy ($U$)!

topics.title: Thermometry Scales, Linear/Area/Volume Thermal Expansion, Pendulum Clocks & Thermal Stress
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Thermometry & Universal Scale Conversion
How Any Linear Thermometer Scale Works:
Between the Ice Point (Lower Fixed Point, $\text{LFP}$) and Steam Point (Upper Fixed Point, $\text{UFP}$), the fractional rise of any temperature reading $X$ is identical across all scales:
$$\boxed{\frac{X - \text{LFP}}{\text{UFP} - \text{LFP}} = \frac{T_C - 0}{100 - 0} = \frac{T_F - 32}{212 - 32} = \frac{T_K - 273.15}{373.15 - 273.15}}$$
$$\text{For Temperature Differences } (\Delta T): \quad \boxed{\Delta T_C = \Delta T_K = \frac{5}{9}\Delta T_F}$$
1.2 Thermal Expansion of Solids ($\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$)

Why do solids expand when heated? Because the potential energy curve $U(r)$ between neighbouring atoms is asymmetric (steeper for compression than for stretching). As thermal vibrations increase, the average interatomic separation shifts outward!

Expansion TypeDefining FormulaRelation Among Coefficients (Isotropic Solid)
1. Linear Expansion ($\alpha$)$L = L_0(1 + \alpha \Delta T)$Base coefficient $\alpha$ (Unit: $\text{K}^{-1}$ or $^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$)
2. Superficial / Area ($\beta$)$A = A_0(1 + \beta \Delta T)$$\beta = 2\alpha$ (For anisotropic: $\beta = \alpha_x + \alpha_y$)
3. Volumetric / Cubical ($\gamma$)$V = V_0(1 + \gamma \Delta T)$$\gamma = 3\alpha$ (Hence $\boxed{\alpha : \beta : \gamma = 1 : 2 : 3}$)

3 Classic JEE Applications of Thermal Expansion:

  • 1. Metal Pendulum Clock Time Loss/Gain: Since $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g} \propto L^{1/2}$, by Binomial Approximation:
    $$\boxed{\frac{\Delta T}{T} = \frac{1}{2}\alpha \Delta\theta} \qquad \left(\text{Time lost per day } (86400\text{ s}) = \frac{1}{2}\alpha \Delta\theta \times 86400\text{ s}\right)$$
  • 2. Thermal Stress in a Clamped Rod: If a rod of Young's modulus $Y$ is rigidly clamped between two walls so its length cannot expand ($\epsilon = \alpha\Delta T$):
    $$\boxed{\text{Thermal Stress } \sigma = Y \alpha \Delta T \implies \text{Compressive Force } F = Y A \alpha \Delta T}$$
  • 3. Variation of Density with Temperature: Since mass $m$ is constant and $V = V_0(1 + \gamma\Delta T)$:
    $$\boxed{\rho = \frac{\rho_0}{1 + \gamma\Delta T} \approx \rho_0(1 - \gamma\Delta T)}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Proof that β = 2α and γ = 3α Using Binomial Approximation

Consider a square plate of side $L_0$. When heated by $\Delta T$, its new side is $L = L_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$. Its new area is:

$$A = L^2 = L_0^2(1 + \alpha\Delta T)^2 = A_0(1 + 2\alpha\Delta T + \alpha^2(\Delta T)^2)$$

Since $\alpha \sim 10^{-5}\text{ K}^{-1}$, the quadratic term $\alpha^2(\Delta T)^2 \sim 10^{-8}$ is negligible, leaving $A \approx A_0(1 + 2\alpha\Delta T) \implies \boxed{\beta = 2\alpha}$. Similarly, cubing $L = L_0(1+\alpha\Delta T)$ gives $V \approx V_0(1 + 3\alpha\Delta T) \implies \boxed{\gamma = 3\alpha}$.

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Does a Cavity or Hole Inside a Metal Plate Shrink or Expand When Heated?): Students often think the metal expands inward and makes the hole smaller. WRONG! Thermal expansion is exactly like a photographic enlargement (zooming in on a picture). Every single linear dimension—including the diameter of holes, cavities, and the gap in a C-ring—expands outward by the exact same factor $(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$!
  • Trap 2 (Anomalous Expansion of Water between $0^\circ\text{C}$ and $4^\circ\text{C}$): When water is heated from $0^\circ\text{C}$ to $4^\circ\text{C}$, it contracts instead of expanding, reaching its minimum volume and maximum density ($1000\text{ kg/m}^3$) at $4^\circ\text{C}$! Above $4^\circ\text{C}$, it expands normally.

topics.title: Calorimetry: Specific Heat, Latent Heat of Fusion/Vaporization, Heating Curves & Ice-Water-Steam Mixing
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Sensible Heat ($Q = ms\Delta T$) vs. Latent Heat ($Q = mL$)
Principle of Calorimetry (Conservation of Thermal Energy):
When two or more bodies at different temperatures are mixed inside an insulated calorimeter with no heat loss to the surroundings: $$\boxed{\text{Total Heat Lost by Hot Bodies} = \text{Total Heat Gained by Cold Bodies}}$$
Heat TypeFormulaPhysical Effect & Water Constants to Memorize
1. Specific Heat ($s$)
(Temperature Change, Same Phase)		$$Q = m s \Delta T$$Changes temperature without changing state.
• $s_{\text{water}} = 1\text{ cal g}^{-1}\,^\circ\text{C}^{-1} = 4200\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$
• $s_{\text{ice}} = s_{\text{steam}} = 0.5\text{ cal g}^{-1}\,^\circ\text{C}^{-1} = 2100\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$
2. Latent Heat ($L$)
(Phase Change at Constant $T$)		$$Q = m L$$Breaks intermolecular bonds at constant temperature!
• Latent heat of fusion of ice: $L_f = 80\text{ cal/g} = 3.36 \times 10^5\text{ J/kg}$
• Latent heat of vaporization of steam: $L_v = 540\text{ cal/g} = 2.26 \times 10^6\text{ J/kg}$

Water Equivalent ($W$) of a Calorimeter Vessel: The mass of water that would absorb the same amount of heat per degree rise as the vessel: $\boxed{W = \frac{m_{\text{vessel}} s_{\text{vessel}}}{s_{\text{water}}}}$.
topics.derivationHtml:
Step-by-Step Algorithm for Ice–Water–Steam Mixing Problems (Never Guess the Final State!)

Suppose $m_{\text{ice}}$ grams of ice at $0^\circ\text{C}$ is mixed with $m_{\text{water}}$ grams of water at $T_w^\circ\text{C}$. How do you know if all the ice melts?

Step 1: Calculate the maximum heat the hot water can release when cooled all the way to $0^\circ\text{C}$: $Q_{\text{available}} = m_{\text{water}} (1) (T_w - 0)\text{ cal}$.

Step 2: Calculate the heat required to melt all the ice at $0^\circ\text{C}$: $Q_{\text{needed}} = m_{\text{ice}} \times 80\text{ cal}$.

Step 3 (Compare $Q_{\text{available}}$ vs. $Q_{\text{needed}}$):
• If $Q_{\text{available}} < Q_{\text{needed}}$: Not all ice melts! The final equilibrium temperature is strictly $T_{\text{final}} = 0^\circ\text{C}$, and the mass of ice that melts is $m_{\text{melted}} = \frac{Q_{\text{available}}}{80}$.
• If $Q_{\text{available}} > Q_{\text{needed}}$: All ice melts into water at $0^\circ\text{C}$, and the leftover heat $(Q_{\text{available}} - Q_{\text{needed}})$ warms the total water $(m_{\text{ice}} + m_{\text{water}})$ to $T_{\text{final}} = \frac{Q_{\text{available}} - Q_{\text{needed}}}{m_{\text{ice}} + m_{\text{water}}}$!

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Slope of $T$ vs. $Q$ Heating Graph): Since $\Delta Q = ms\Delta T \implies \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta Q} = \frac{1}{ms}$, the slope of a Temperature vs. Heat graph is inversely proportional to specific heat capacity $s$! Steeper slope means smaller specific heat; longer horizontal flat plateau means larger latent heat ($L_v = 540 > L_f = 80$).

topics.title: Heat Transfer I — Conduction: Fourier's Law, Thermal Resistance, Series/Parallel Rods & Growth of Ice on Ponds
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Fourier's Law of Heat Conduction & The Ohm's Law Electrical Analogy
Steady State Conduction:
In steady state, the temperature of every cross-section of a lagged rod becomes constant in time, and the heat current $H = \frac{dQ}{dt}$ flowing into any cross-section equals the heat current flowing out!
$$\text{Heat Current:} \quad \boxed{H = \frac{dQ}{dt} = -K A \frac{dT}{dx} = \frac{K A (T_1 - T_2)}{L} = \frac{\Delta T}{R_{\text{th}}}} \qquad \left(\text{Thermal Resistance } \boxed{R_{\text{th}} = \frac{L}{K A}}\right)$$
Electrical Quantity (Ohm's Law)Thermal Conduction Equivalent
Electric Current $I = \frac{dq}{dt}$Heat Current $H = \frac{dQ}{dt}$ (Watts, $\text{J/s}$)
Potential Difference $V_1 - V_2$Temperature Difference $T_1 - T_2$ ($\text{K}$ or $^\circ\text{C}$)
Electrical Resistance $R = \frac{L}{\sigma A}$Thermal Resistance $R_{\text{th}} = \frac{L}{K A}$ ($\text{K/W}$)
Series Rods: $R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 + R_2$$$K_{\text{eq, series}} = \frac{L_1 + L_2}{\frac{L_1}{K_1} + \frac{L_2}{K_2}} \quad \left(\text{For } L_1 = L_2: \; \frac{2K_1 K_2}{K_1 + K_2}\right)$$
Parallel Rods: $\frac{1}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}$$$K_{\text{eq, parallel}} = \frac{K_1 A_1 + K_2 A_2}{A_1 + A_2} \quad \left(\text{For } A_1 = A_2: \; \frac{K_1 + K_2}{2}\right)$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Classic JEE Derivation: Rate of Growth of Ice Thickness on a Frozen Lake

Suppose air above a lake is at sub-zero temperature $-\theta^\circ\text{C}$, while water below the ice is at $0^\circ\text{C}$. At time $t$, the ice layer has thickness $y$. For an additional thickness $dy$ to freeze in time $dt$, latent heat $dQ = (\rho A\,dy)L_f$ must conduct upward through thickness $y$:

$$\frac{dQ}{dt} = (\rho A L_f)\frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{K A (0 - (-\theta))}{y}$$

Separating variables and integrating from $y = y_1$ to $y = y_2$:

$$\int_{y_1}^{y_2} y\,dy = \frac{K\theta}{\rho L_f}\int_0^t dt \implies \boxed{t = \frac{\rho L_f}{2K\theta}\left(y_2^2 - y_1^2\right) \implies y \propto \sqrt{t}}$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Ice Thickness Ratio): Since $t \propto y^2$, if it takes $t_1 = 1\text{ hour}$ to form the first $1\text{ cm}$ of ice ($y=0$ to $1\text{ cm}$), forming the next $1\text{ cm}$ of ice ($y=1\text{ cm}$ to $2\text{ cm}$) takes $t_2 \propto (2^2 - 1^2) = \mathbf{3\text{ hours}}$, NOT $1\text{ hour}$!

topics.title: Heat Transfer II — Thermal Radiation: Kirchhoff's Law, Stefan-Boltzmann Law, Wien's Displacement Law & Newton's Law of Cooling
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 Blackbody Radiation, Stefan-Boltzmann Law & Wien's Displacement Law
Ideal Blackbody & Kirchhoff's Law:
An ideal blackbody absorbs $100\%$ of all incident radiation ($a = 1, e = 1$). Kirchhoff's Law states that good absorbers at a given wavelength are also good emitters at that wavelength ($E_\lambda / a_\lambda = E_{\lambda,\text{blackbody}}$).
$$\textbf{1. Stefan-Boltzmann Law (Radiated Power):} \quad \boxed{P = \frac{dQ}{dt} = e \sigma A T^4} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Net Loss in Surroundings } T_0: \; \boxed{P_{\text{net}} = e \sigma A (T^4 - T_0^4)}$$

Where $\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\text{ W m}^{-2}\text{ K}^{-4}$ is Stefan's constant, $e \in [0, 1]$ is emissivity, and $T$ is strictly in Kelvin (K)!

$$\textbf{2. Wien's Displacement Law (Peak Wavelength } \lambda_m\text{):} \quad \boxed{\lambda_m T = b = \text{Constant}} \qquad \left(b \approx 2.898 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\cdot\text{K}\right)$$
4.2 Newton's Law of Cooling (Exact & Average Forms)
Condition:
When the temperature difference between a hot body ($T$) and its surroundings ($T_0$) is small, the rate of cooling ($-\frac{dT}{dt}$) is directly proportional to $(T - T_0)$:
$$\text{1. Differential Form:} \quad \boxed{-\frac{dT}{dt} = k(T - T_0)} \qquad \left(\text{where } k = \frac{4 e \sigma A T_0^3}{ms}\right)$$
$$\text{2. Average Numerical Form (Most Used in JEE!):} \quad \boxed{\frac{T_1 - T_2}{t} = k\left(\frac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_0\right)}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
How Stefan's T⁴ Law Reduces to Newton's Linear Cooling Law for Small ΔT

Let body temperature be $T = T_0 + \Delta T$ where $\Delta T \ll T_0$. By Stefan's Law, net rate of heat loss is $ms\left(-\frac{dT}{dt}\right) = e\sigma A (T^4 - T_0^4)$:

$$T^4 - T_0^4 = (T_0 + \Delta T)^4 - T_0^4 = T_0^4\left[\left(1 + \frac{\Delta T}{T_0}\right)^4 - 1\right] \approx T_0^4\left[1 + 4\frac{\Delta T}{T_0} - 1\right] = 4 T_0^3 \Delta T = 4 T_0^3 (T - T_0)$$

Therefore, $\boxed{-\frac{dT}{dt} = \left(\frac{4e\sigma A T_0^3}{ms}\right)(T - T_0) = k(T - T_0)}$!

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Putting Celsius into Stefan's $T^4$ or Wien's $\lambda_m T = b$): In radiation laws, $T$ MUST be in absolute Kelvin ($T_K = T_C + 273$)! For example, $27^\circ\text{C} = 300\text{ K}$ and $127^\circ\text{C} = 400\text{ K}$.
  • Trap 2 (Rate of Heat Loss $dQ/dt$ vs. Rate of Cooling $-dT/dt$): If two solid spheres of the same material and same surface temperature $T$ have radii $r_1$ and $r_2$:
    • Rate of Heat Loss ($dQ/dt = e\sigma A(T^4 - T_0^4)$) is proportional to surface area $A \propto r^2$.
    • Rate of Cooling ($-dT/dt = \frac{dQ/dt}{ms}$) is proportional to $\frac{A}{V} = \frac{4\pi r^2}{\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3} \propto \mathbf{\frac{1}{r}}$! Thus the smaller sphere cools down faster in degrees per second!

conclusion: You have mastered Chapter 10: Thermal Properties of Matter! You are now ready to study how thermal energy is converted into mechanical work in Chapter 11: Thermodynamics.
summary:
• Expansion: $\beta = 2\alpha$, $\gamma = 3\alpha$; Pendulum $\Delta T/T = \frac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta\theta$; Thermal stress $\sigma = Y\alpha\Delta T$.
  • Calorimetry: $Q = ms\Delta T$ (temperature change) and $Q = mL$ (phase change at constant $T$).
  • Conduction: $H = \frac{\Delta T}{R_{\text{th}}}$ where $R_{\text{th}} = \frac{L}{KA}$; Ice growth $t = \frac{\rho L_f}{2K\theta}(y_2^2 - y_1^2)$.
  • Radiation: Stefan $P = e\sigma A(T^4 - T_0^4)$; Wien $\lambda_m T = b$; Newton cooling $\frac{T_1 - T_2}{t} = k\left(\frac{T_1+T_2}{2} - T_0\right)$.

Series Thermal Conductivity$K_{\text{eq}} = \dfrac{L_1 + L_2}{\frac{L_1}{K_1} + \frac{L_2}{K_2}}$Harmonic mean $\dfrac{2K_1 K_2}{K_1+K_2}$ if $L_1 = L_2$.

questions.prompt: At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales read the exact same numerical value?

How much heat in calories is required to convert $10\text{ g}$ of ice at $-10^\circ\text{C}$ completely into steam at $100^\circ\text{C}$? ($s_{\text{ice}} = 0.5\text{ cal/g}^\circ\text{C}$, $L_f = 80\text{ cal/g}$, $s_{\text{water}} = 1\text{ cal/g}^\circ\text{C}$, $L_v = 540\text{ cal/g}$)
questions.explanation: Add the 4 stages: (1) Ice $-10^\circ\text{C} \to 0^\circ\text{C}$: $10(0.5)(10) = 50\text{ cal}$. (2) Melt ice at $0^\circ\text{C}$: $10(80) = 800\text{ cal}$. (3) Water $0^\circ\text{C} \to 100^\circ\text{C}$: $10(1)(100) = 1000\text{ cal}$. (4) Boil to steam at $100^\circ\text{C}$: $10(540) = 5400\text{ cal}$. Total $= 50 + 800 + 1000 + 5400 = 7250\text{ cal}$.

questions.prompt: A body cools from $60^\circ\text{C}$ to $50^\circ\text{C}$ in $10\text{ minutes}$ when the surrounding room temperature is $25^\circ\text{C}$. What will be its temperature at the end of the next $10\text{ minutes}$?
questions.explanation: First interval: $\frac{60 - 50}{10} = k\left(\frac{60+50}{2} - 25\right) \implies 1 = 30k \implies k = \frac{1}{30}$. Second interval (from $50^\circ\text{C}$ to $T$): $\frac{50 - T}{10} = \frac{1}{30}\left(\frac{50 + T}{2} - 25\right) = \frac{T}{60} \implies 6(50 - T) = T \implies 300 = 7T \implies T = \frac{300}{7} \approx 42.85^\circ\text{C}$.

questions.prompt: Two rods of identical dimensions having thermal conductivities $K_1 = 60\text{ W/m}\cdot\text{K}$ and $K_2 = 40\text{ W/m}\cdot\text{K}$ are joined end-to-end in series. What is the equivalent thermal conductivity $K_{\text{eq}}$ of the composite rod?
questions.explanation: For two equal-length rods in series, $K_{\text{eq}} = \frac{2K_1 K_2}{K_1 + K_2} = \frac{2(60)(40)}{60 + 40} = \frac{4800}{100} = 48\text{ W/m}\cdot\text{K}$.

questions.prompt: If the temperature of a blackbody is increased by $50\%$ (from $T$ to $1.5T$), by what percentage does the rate of energy radiated by it increase?
questions.explanation: By Stefan's Law, $P \propto T^4$. When $T' = 1.5T = \frac{3}{2}T$, the new power is $P' = \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^4 P = \frac{81}{16}P = 5.0625 P$. Therefore, the percentage increase is $(5.0625 - 1) \times 100\% = 406.25\%$.

questions.prompt: 50 g of ice at $0^\circ\text{C}$ is mixed with 50 g of water at $60^\circ\text{C}$ in an insulated vessel. What is the final temperature of the mixture, and how much ice remains unmelted?
options: Final T = 0°C, 12.5 g of ice remains unmelted
Final T = 0°C, 25 g of ice remains unmelted
questions.answer: Final T = 0°C, 12.5 g of ice remains unmelted
questions.explanation: Heat available from cooling 50 g of water from $60^\circ\text{C}$ to $0^\circ\text{C}$ is $Q_{\text{avail}} = 50(1)(60) = 3000\text{ cal}$. Heat required to melt all 50 g of ice is $Q_{\text{needed}} = 50(80) = 4000\text{ cal}$. Since $Q_{\text{avail}} < Q_{\text{needed}}$, final temperature stays at $0^\circ\text{C}$! Mass of ice melted $= \frac{3000}{80} = 37.5\text{ g}$, so $50 - 37.5 = 12.5\text{ g}$ of ice remains unmelted.
